scLimbsCoveredByACT: NOTE ON CORPUS SHAPE: SC 3.3.2 has 0 ACT rules and 0 ACT test cases (confirmed in eval/act-augmented/_resources/3.3.2.json and index.json: actRuleCount 0, testCaseCount 0, testCaseCountsByExpected {}). The ONLY first-party ACT-corpus material is 8 WCAG technique docs (7 web + 1 PDF). So every 'covered' limb below is covered only at the technique-prose level, never by an executable ACT rule or a pass/fail test-case page. There is no machine-runnable corpus for this SC at all.

Core obligation 'present labels or instructions that identify the controls in a form so that users know what input data is expected' (Understanding intent para 1) - covered as the central theme of G131 (descriptive labels make the component's purpose clear), H44 (label elements associate text labels with controls), and PDF10 (labels for PDF form controls).

Labels for individual OPTIONS within radio buttons / checkboxes / comboboxes 'so that users know what they are actually selecting' (intent para 1) - covered by H44 (per-option <label> for each radio/checkbox example: doughnut radios, computerskills checkbox) and H71 (Hamlet multiple-choice radios, interests checkboxes each with their own <label>).

Instructions specifying DATA FORMATS for entry fields, 'especially if they are out of the customary formats or if there are specific rules for correct input' (intent para 1) - covered by the Understanding Examples (date-format instruction; username character-rule instruction) and by PDF10's tooltip example ('Date you are available: use MM/DD/YYYY format'). Note: present only as example prose, no test page.

Image-based / graphical labels are acceptable if 'widely understood by the intended target audience' (intent para 3) - covered by G167 (magnify-glass loupe icon and paper-airplane 'send message' icon serving as visible labels for search / message fields) and named in the Understanding global-search example.

Required-field identification (Benefits bullet 2; intent 'requires = accepts/expects, applies to all fields') - covered by G131 ('label may include text or a text symbol indicating that input is required'; 'required' in parentheses example) and ARIA2 (asterisk-in-label, '(required)' text, aria-required supplementing a VISIBLE indicator).

Group-level labels for multi-field constructs where a single label is insufficient (intent radio/checkbox grouping; the phone-number and Given/Family-name Examples) - covered by H71 (fieldset/legend for radio groups, checkbox groups, and address groups) and by F82 (failure: phone-number fields with NO group text label) referencing H71.

Adjacent-button-as-label pattern (search field labeled by 'Search' button; chat reply labeled by send button) - covered by G167 as a sufficient technique with search, send-message, and 'Get Form for State' dropdown examples.

Describing what will happen BEFORE a change to a form control that causes a change of context (an 'instruction' under 3.3.2) - covered by G13 (advisory): language-select dropdown and auto-advance survey examples.

A genuine FAILING construction exists in prose: F82 (visually formatted phone-number fields with no text label / no instructions) - this is the one technique that yields a concrete fail pattern, and the local SEED file (_seeds/by-sc/3.3.2.json) operationalizes 8 real-world failing patterns (placeholder-as-only-label, color/asterisk-only required marking, ungrouped custom radios).

The 4.1.2-vs-3.3.2 distinction (a control can have an aria-label and pass 4.1.2 yet fail 3.3.2 if the label is not presented VISUALLY to all users) - stated in the Understanding intent and reinforced by H44's note that for 3.3.2 the <label> 'must be visible' (unlike for 1.1.1/1.3.1/4.1.2 where it may be CSS-hidden), and by ARIA2's note that aria-required alone without a visual indicator does not meet 3.3.2.
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: NO ACT RULE AND NO TEST CASE EXISTS - the single largest gap. Unlike SCs with ACT rules, 3.3.2 has zero executable rules and zero pass/fail/inapplicable fixture pages in the corpus. There is nothing to sample 'across rules'; the only corpus artifacts are 8 static technique HTML docs plus the 8-pattern local seed file. Every variety claim below is about technique-prose coverage, not test-case coverage.

The 'visible WHEN THE FIELD HAS FOCUS' limb - the Understanding ('make such instructions available to users only when the individual control has focus, especially when instructions are long and verbose') and Trusted Tester ('The label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus') both treat focus-revealed instructions as a first-class, ACCEPTABLE pattern. No technique demonstrates or tests a focus-revealed-instruction page; this dynamic/behavioral limb is entirely absent from the techniques.

The 'too much information is as harmful as too little / do not clutter the page' limb (intent para 2) - the requirement that instructions be SUFFICIENT but not excessive. No technique or test addresses over-labeling / redundant-instruction failure or the 'enough to accomplish the task without undue confusion' balance.

Image-label ADEQUACY caveat: the intent says image labels must be 'widely understood by the intended target audience' and recommends supplementary text/tooltips for clarity. The techniques (G167) only show the happy path (well-understood loupe/airplane icons); there is NO coverage of an obscure/ambiguous icon label that would FAIL because the audience cannot interpret it.

Scope EXCLUSION limb - 'This success criterion does not apply to links or other controls (expand/collapse widget, etc.) that are not associated with data entry.' No technique or inapplicable case demonstrates a non-data-entry control correctly being out of scope (the boundary that prevents false positives). Trusted Tester's 'DNA if no form elements / all disabled' and the EN 'Not applicable' branch are likewise unexercised by any fixture.

Disabled / read-only field handling - Trusted Tester explicitly EXCLUDES disabled inputs and includes read-only fields as in-scope form components. No technique covers either the disabled-exclusion or the read-only-inclusion edge.

Instructions delivered as separate page-level prose vs. inline-per-field - G13 mentions instructions in reading order, multi-step processes, and training, but there is no technique showing a global/standalone instruction block that legitimately satisfies several fields, nor a test of its reading-order positioning relative to the controls.

Comboboxes / select menus as the labeled control - the intent names 'comboboxes' alongside radios/checkboxes, but H44/H71 examples center on text inputs, radios, and checkboxes. <select>/combobox option-labeling and listbox-option labeling are not exemplified.

Non-HTML, non-PDF technologies - the SC is technology-agnostic (EN applies it to non-web documents C.10 and software C.11). Only HTML (H44/H71), generic (G13/G131/G167), ARIA (ARIA2), and PDF (PDF10) appear. No native-app, SVG-form, or canvas/custom-widget labeling coverage.

Format-instruction FAILURE construction - while the date/username-format instruction is named as an example, there is no failure technique for an out-of-customary-format field (e.g., an unusual date or password-rule field) presented with NO format instruction. The only concrete failure prose is F82, which is narrowly the phone-number group-label case.
contentDomainsPresent: Form text inputs - first/last name, login name, password, account number, email, address/zip (H44, ARIA2, H71)
Radio-button groups - doughnut flavor selection, Hamlet multiple-choice quiz, balance-alert radiogroup (H44, H71, ARIA2)
Grouped multi-field constructs - residential vs postal address fieldsets, US phone-number (area/exchange/number) fields (H71, F82)
Required-field marking - asterisk-in-label, '(required)' text, CSS ::after star icon, red-border styling, aria-required (ARIA2, G131)
Search fields with icon/button labels - magnify-glass loupe, adjacent 'Search' button (G167)
Messaging/chat compose field labeled by a send-message (paper-airplane) icon button (G167)
Dropdown/select controls that change context - language selector, state-form picker, auto-advance survey (G13, G167)
PDF interactive forms - tooltip (TU entry) labels, e.g. availability-date field with MM/DD/YYYY instruction (PDF10)
Date-entry and username fields with format/character-rule instructions (Understanding Examples)

Real-world platform failure domains from the local seed file - Squarespace/Wix/Divi/Elementor/Bubble/Webflow/Shopify/HubSpot/Gravity contact, checkout, booking, and newsletter forms with placeholder-as-label and color-only required markers
varietyGaps: BIGGEST GAP - there is no executable ACT rule and no pass/fail/inapplicable test-case page for 3.3.2 at all; the entire 'corpus' is 8 static technique docs (7 HTML/generic/ARIA + 1 PDF) plus an 8-pattern local seed list. A harness cannot sample fail/pass/inapplicable outcomes for this SC from the ACT corpus because none exist (testCaseCountsByExpected = {}).

OUTCOME imbalance - the technique docs are overwhelmingly PASS/sufficient demonstrations (G131, G167, H44, H71, PDF10, ARIA2). Exactly ONE failure artifact exists (F82, narrowly phone-number group labels). There are no failing exemplars for the most common real-world 3.3.2 break - the placeholder-as-only-label input - even though the local seed file says that is the dominant field failure. Pass-heavy, almost no fail variety.

DYNAMIC / BEHAVIORAL gap - 3.3.2 explicitly blesses focus-revealed instructions and the 'label disappears once you type a placeholder' failure is the dominant real failure mode (per the seed file). Neither focus-reveal (pass) nor placeholder-vanish-on-input (fail) is representable by the static technique pages; this is the static-vs-dynamic gap flagged in MEMORY (held-out generalization).

The LABELS-vs-INSTRUCTIONS split is lopsided toward labels - 6 of 8 techniques concern LABELS (H44, H71, G131, G167, ARIA2, PDF10). Only G13 covers INSTRUCTIONS, and only the change-of-context flavor; data-FORMAT instructions and required/rule instructions exist only as Understanding example prose with no technique or page. The 'instructions' half of the SC is thinly represented.

Scope-boundary / inapplicable variety is entirely missing - no artifact exercises the exclusions that prevent false positives: links and non-data-entry widgets (expand/collapse), disabled inputs, or pages with no form elements (TT 'DNA' / EN 'Not applicable'). A grader has nothing to learn the negative boundary from.

Technology variety is narrow - HTML + generic + ARIA + PDF only. No coverage of native software/SVG/canvas/custom-component form labeling despite the SC and EN (C.10/C.11) being technology-agnostic; combobox/<select> option-labeling is also unexemplified.

Adequacy/contrast confounds are out-of-scope by design but lurk - the SC is strictly 'is a visible label/instruction PRESENT' (TT note: adequacy is 2.4.6, association is 1.3.1/4.1.2). The corpus offers no clean isolating case that passes 3.3.2 while deliberately failing a neighbor SC (e.g., present-but-CSS-hidden label = passes 4.1.2, fails 3.3.2), so the cross-SC isolation that the Understanding stresses is never demonstrated by a page.

Image/icon-label NEGATIVE case missing - only well-understood icons (loupe, paper airplane) are shown; no ambiguous-icon-label failure exists to test the 'widely understood by the target audience' qualifier.

aspects.title: Instruction promised on focus does not actually become perceivable when the field is focused
aspects.description: WCAG explicitly blesses the pattern of withholding a long/verbose instruction until the field receives focus, and Trusted Tester makes 'visible when the form field has focus' a normative requirement. The conformance question is therefore behavioral: when the field is focused, does the promised instruction (password-complexity rule, date-format hint, character rules) actually become visible? The failure is a field whose only instruction is wired to appear on focus but in fact (a) never appears, (b) appears empty/placeholder-only, (c) appears off-screen / clipped / behind another element, (d) auto-dismisses before the user can read or act on it, or (e) requires hover (not keyboard focus) so keyboard users never get it. The static DOM looks fine; only driving the focus state and visually judging the rendered result reveals whether the instruction is honored. This is the entire 'available only when the individual control has focus' limb operationalized as a failure.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 1 — instructions may be made available only when the individual control has focus (especially when long/verbose); TT note — the label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.
aspects.whyUncovered: There are zero ACT rules and zero test-case pages for 3.3.2, so nothing exercises any dynamic state. All 8 technique docs show static, always-visible labels; none demonstrates a focus-revealed instruction, let alone one that fails to appear, time out, or trigger on hover instead of focus. The 8-pattern seed file is entirely about placeholder/required/grouping in the static DOM. A linter inspecting static HTML sees the instruction node (or a :focus CSS rule) present and reports a label exists; it cannot drive focus, observe what actually renders, time the appearance/disappearance, distinguish a :hover trigger from a :focus trigger, or judge whether the focused instruction is genuinely perceivable. This requires interacting with the page and visually judging the focused state.

references.quote: Content authors may also choose to make such instructions available to users only when the individual control has focus especially when instructions are long and verbose.
The label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages with a small JS/CSS focus mechanism on a single data-entry field whose ONLY instruction is focus-gated, then break the mechanism in a distinct way per page. Each page must render the instruction correctly OR fail in exactly one observable way detectable only by tabbing to the field. Provide a visible static heading so the page is judgeable, and ensure no always-visible label duplicates the focus-only instruction (otherwise the field would pass on the static label). Vision verification must screenshot the focused state, not just the default state.
suggestedScenarios: Password field whose complexity rules ('8+ chars, 1 number, 1 symbol') are wired to reveal on focus, but a handler typo means the rules div never un-hides — on focus the field shows only empty space where instructions should be.
Coupon-code field whose format hint ('Format: ABC-1234') is set to display only on :hover (not :focus), so a keyboard user tabbing to the field gets no instruction while a mouse user does.
Date field whose 'use MM/DD/YYYY' hint appears on focus but is absolutely positioned behind a fixed footer/overlay, so when focused the hint is rendered fully occluded / off-screen.

Username field whose on-focus instruction tooltip fades in then auto-dismisses after 1.5s via a timer, vanishing before a slow reader finishes and never returning unless the field is blurred and re-focused.

Multi-field form where every field reveals its instruction on focus correctly EXCEPT the 'security answer' field, whose reveal is gated on a state variable that is never true, so it silently stays hidden while the rest of the form looks consistent.
A 'tax ID' field whose focus-revealed hint appears but contains only a non-breaking-space placeholder (the real text was never populated), so something flickers in on focus but conveys nothing.

aspects.title: Instruction is present and well-formatted but semantically wrong, stale, or contradicts the field's actual rule
aspects.description: 3.3.2 requires instructions that identify the controls so users know what input data is expected and that specify data formats, especially out-of-customary formats or specific input rules. A field can DISPLAY a confident, perfectly-marked-up instruction that is simply incorrect or stale relative to what the field accepts: the visible hint says 'MM/DD/YYYY' but the field enforces DD/MM/YYYY; 'Max 20 characters' while it truncates at 10; 'Enter your 5-digit ZIP' next to a field requiring ZIP+4; or copied boilerplate naming the wrong purpose entirely ('Enter your member ID' on a promo-code field). The user is actively misled — following the instruction guarantees an error — which the Understanding warns is as harmful as too little. The label/instruction is structurally perfect; the defect is purely the correspondence between the words and the field's real behavior.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 1 — instructions/labels may specify data formats, especially out-of-customary formats or specific rules for correct input; intent para 2 — too much information or instruction can be just as harmful as too little.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists; the technique examples only show instructions correct by construction (the date-format example, the username-rules example). There is no failure technique for a wrong/stale instruction and no seed pattern covers content that is present-but-false (the seeds are all about missing/placeholder/color-only labels). Automated tools verify the existence and association of label text; they have no model of what the field actually accepts (the pattern/maxlength/validation logic vs. the prose) to compare against, so they cannot detect a contradiction between a hint and the field's behavior. Catching this requires reading the instruction, inferring the rule, and noticing the conflict.

references.quote: Instructions or labels may also specify data formats for data entry fields, especially if they are out of the customary formats or if there are specific rules for correct input.

Too much information or instruction can be just as harmful as too little. The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages where each data-entry field carries a visible, correctly-associated instruction that demonstrably conflicts with the field's enforced rule. Make the conflict concrete and verifiable from the page itself: encode the real rule in pattern/maxlength/min-max or in a small inline validator, and write a visible hint that contradicts it. The defect must be discoverable by reading the hint, inferring the enforced rule, and noticing they disagree — not by any missing-label check. Include at least one always-correct control on each page as a contrast so the page is not uniformly broken.
suggestedScenarios: Date-of-birth field whose visible hint reads 'Format: MM/DD/YYYY' but whose maxlength and pattern enforce DD/MM/YYYY, so any user who literally follows the instruction is rejected.
'Verification code' field with helper text 'Enter the 6-digit code' next to an input with maxlength='4' that only accepts 4 digits.
Password field whose instruction says 'Must be at least 8 characters' but whose pattern requires 12, so a compliant-per-instruction password fails.
Phone field with fieldset legend 'Phone number (US, 10 digits)' on a checkout that actually requires the 11-digit country-code form — the group label understates the real requirement.
Coupon field whose instruction was copied from another form and still reads 'Enter your member ID' even though the field is now for a promo code, naming the wrong purpose entirely.
Currency field hinted 'Enter amount in dollars (e.g. 25.00)' whose validator rejects decimals and accepts only whole dollars, so the worked example given is itself invalid.

aspects.title: Image-only / icon-only label that is not 'widely understood by the intended target audience'
aspects.description: The Understanding accepts images as labels but adds the explicit caveat that authors must ensure the images are widely understood by the intended target audience, recommending supplementary tooltips/text for clarity. G167's happy path uses near-universal icons (magnify glass, paper-airplane send). The uncovered failure is a data-entry field whose ONLY visible cue is an ambiguous, decorative, or domain-obscure glyph — a lone '#' next to a field secretly meaning 'enter quantity', a generic gear/sliders icon as the only cue for a 'budget' field, two adjacent fields each cued by indistinguishable icons. A sighted user cannot tell what to type. This is a 3.3.2 visible-cue-adequacy failure even if the icon carries correct alt text giving it an accessible name (which would pass 4.1.2) — the visible cue still fails to communicate purpose to everyone.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 3 — using images as labels meets the criterion only if the images are widely understood by the intended target audience; TT note — the label or instruction can be graphical or textual.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists, and G167 only documents well-understood icons; there is no failure technique for an obscure icon and no seed pattern covers image-label adequacy (seeds are all text/placeholder/color cases). Tools can confirm an icon has alt text / an accessible name, but they have no notion of whether the rendered GLYPH is interpretable by a human looking at it. 'Widely understood by the intended target audience' is an irreducibly human, audience-relative semantic judgment that requires actually viewing the icon and reasoning about what a typical user would infer.

references.quote: Using images as labels meets the requirements of the criterion, but care should be taken to ensure that the images are widely understood by the intended target audience. Authors may consider providing additional hints, such as text-based tooltips or supplementary text, to support clarity when using image-based labels.
The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages where a data-entry field's ONLY visible label is a graphical glyph (inline SVG or icon font), deliberately chosen to be ambiguous, decorative, or domain-obscure for that field's purpose. To isolate this from 4.1.2, give the icon a plausible accessible name (alt/aria-label) so a linter sees a name present — the failure is that a sighted user cannot infer the field's purpose from the rendered glyph. Render icons at realistic small sizes and include at least one near-universal icon (magnify glass) as a passing contrast so 'icon labels' are not flagged wholesale. Vision verification must judge interpretability of the glyph as rendered.
suggestedScenarios: Profile form where the only visible cue for a text field is a small lone '#' icon (intended as 'username/handle'), with no text — a sighted user cannot tell whether to enter a number, a tag, or a name.
Settings panel with two adjacent inputs, each labeled only by a near-identical abstract icon (a gear vs. a slightly different gear), so neither field's purpose is visually distinguishable.
Finance form where a field's only cue is a generic 'sliders/equalizer' glyph meant to indicate 'risk tolerance' — an icon not conventionally associated with that meaning.
Field whose only label is a custom company logo glyph (a decorative brand mark) repurposed as the field's icon, carrying no inherent meaning.
Shipping form where a field is cued only by a tiny ambiguous flag/globe icon intended to mean 'country code', with no adjacent text and no tooltip.
Booking form where a single emoji-style glyph (e.g. a clock face) is the sole cue for a field that actually expects a number of guests, not a time.

aspects.title: Group-level (legend/heading) label is needed where individual labels are insufficient, but is absent or only visual — F82 generalized beyond phone numbers
aspects.description: F82 is the one documented failure technique but is narrowly framed around US phone-number fields. The underlying failure generalizes: any set of fields where each field's individual label, read alone, is insufficient and a GROUP-level description is required (H71's core rationale) but the group description is absent or present only as visual proximity/styling, not as a real label. H71 names the test: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that group. The failure is judging that a particular set DOES need a group label and that the visible page fails to provide one. Examples beyond phone: billing vs shipping address blocks with identical inner labels (Street/City/Zip) and no group heading; a split Given/Family name where neither field alone says 'Name'; date-as-three-selects (Day/Month/Year) with no 'Date of birth' grouping.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 1 + examples — options/groups must be labeled so users know what they are selecting; the phone-number and Given/Family-name examples; failure F82 generalized; H71 'an additional heading to provide a description specific to that particular group'.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test page exists. F82 is technique prose limited to phone numbers. The seed file's only grouping pattern is custom radios with broken radiogroup semantics — a different, partly programmatic defect that axe-adjacent tooling and the seed already cover, so this aspect must be constructed with otherwise-correctly-labeled native inputs to avoid duplicating it. Recognizing that a set of fields NEEDS a group label, and that visual proximity is doing work the textual labeling does not, is a contextual semantic judgment about whether the per-field labels are sufficient standalone. Tools can detect a missing fieldset/legend, but presence of fieldset/legend is neither necessary (a visible group heading can suffice) nor a reliable signal of the actual failure (two identical address blocks can each have labeled inputs and pass every linter while being genuinely ambiguous). The 'is a group label needed here?' decision is human.

references.quote: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that particular group, the use of fieldset and legend elements is appropriate.
even if all the fields have programmatically determined names, a text label must also identify the set of fields as a phone number.
Rather than having a single label "Name" (which would appear to leave the second text field unlabelled), each field is given an explicit label — "Given Name" and "Family Name".

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages with sets of NATIVE, individually-labeled inputs (so no missing-label linter fires) that nevertheless need a group-level description which is missing or supplied only by visual spacing/styling. Make the ambiguity concrete: two structurally identical blocks distinguished only by position, or a multi-field construct whose collective purpose is never stated in text. Avoid the seed's broken-radiogroup defect by using correctly-grouped or non-radio constructs. Include at least one page where a proper visible group heading (not fieldset) correctly resolves the ambiguity, as a passing contrast. Vision verification must judge whether a sighted user can tell which block is which / what the set means.
suggestedScenarios: Checkout page with a 'Billing' block and a 'Shipping' block, each containing fields labeled exactly 'Street', 'City', 'Zip' and no visible group heading distinguishing the two — the user cannot tell which block is which.
Date of birth captured as three separate selects whose only labels are 'Day', 'Month', 'Year', with no 'Date of birth' grouping text, so the trio's collective purpose is never stated.
Name captured as two fields both labeled only 'Name' (instead of 'Given name' / 'Family name'), leaving the second field appearing unlabeled per the Understanding's own example.
Credit-card entry split into four fields each labeled only with placeholder dashes and no 'Card number' group label — the four-part grouping conveyed only by visual spacing.
Time-range picker with two adjacent fields each labeled only 'HH:MM' and no 'From'/'To' or 'Available hours' grouping, so the pair's meaning depends entirely on left-to-right order.
Passing contrast: two address blocks each preceded by a visible 'Billing address' / 'Shipping address' heading (no fieldset) that correctly disambiguates the otherwise-identical inner labels.

aspects.title: Format/required instruction exists but is positioned or styled so it is not perceivable as belonging to the field (visually orphaned instruction)
aspects.description: 3.3.2 is about whether the instruction is PRESENTED to all users for that control. A subtle failure: the instruction text genuinely exists and is visible somewhere on the page, but is visually disconnected from the field it governs — placed far above the form, after the submit button, in a collapsed/closed-by-default help panel, in a footnote, or styled so small/low-contrast/greyed that a sighted user does not associate it with (or cannot read) the field. The Understanding warns the goal is to provide enough information to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation; an orphaned instruction forces exactly that navigation. The static text node exists, so a 'does instruction text exist?' check passes; whether a real user perceives it as the field's instruction is a layout/visual judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding 4.1.2-distinction para — labels/instructions must be presented to all users, not just AT users; intent para 2 — enough information without undue confusion or navigation.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists. Technique examples always place the instruction adjacent to or programmatically tied to the field; there is no failure technique for an orphaned instruction, and the seed patterns center on missing/placeholder/color-only labels, not mispositioned-but-present ones. An automated tool searching the DOM for instruction text would FIND it and not flag a problem; tools cannot reason about spatial proximity, reading-order distance, collapsed-disclosure state, contrast-as-it-relates-to-association, or whether a human would visually bind the instruction to the field. This is a perception/layout judgment requiring a rendered view.

references.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).
The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages where each governed field has a real, complete instruction present in the DOM but spatially/visually orphaned from its field in exactly one way per page (distant top-of-form note, post-submit-button placement, collapsed disclosure, tiny low-contrast text, wrong-column proximity). Each field itself should have a proper visible name so no missing-label check fires — the only defect is that the instruction is not perceivably bound to the control. Include a passing contrast where the same instruction sits inline adjacent to its field. Vision verification must judge whether a sighted user would associate the instruction with the field as rendered, not just confirm the text exists.
suggestedScenarios: Long registration form where 'Note: use DD/MM/YYYY for all dates' appears once at the very top, with the date-of-birth field far below and no inline hint, so a user who scrolled past the note has no cue at the point of entry.
Order form whose format instruction for a 'PO number' field lives inside a collapsed '? Help' accordion closed by default, so the instruction is on the page but not visible without an extra click.
Field whose required/format instruction is rendered in 9px light-grey text that, while present, is too small/low-contrast to be read as the field's instruction by a typical sighted user.
Form where the format hint for the 'Tax ID' field is placed AFTER the submit button at the bottom, so in reading/visual order it follows the action rather than informing the field.
Two-column layout where a field's instruction sits in the right column visually adjacent to a DIFFERENT field in the left column, so proximity attaches the instruction to the wrong control.
Passing contrast: the same date-format instruction rendered as readable text immediately beneath its date field, clearly bound to it.

aspects.title: False-positive guard: links and non-data-entry controls correctly out of scope (do not require labels/instructions)
aspects.description: 3.3.2 explicitly does NOT apply to links or other interactive controls that are not associated with data entry (expand/collapse widgets, menu toggles, tabs, pagination links, accordions, dialog-open buttons). The uncovered situation is the INAPPLICABLE / correct-pass case that prevents false positives: a page rich in buttons, links, and disclosure widgets that legitimately have NO field-style instructions because they are not data-entry controls. An evaluator (human or model) must recognize the scope boundary and NOT demand a '3.3.2 instruction' for a non-input control, while still correctly flagging any genuine data-entry field on the same page that lacks instruction. This guards against over-flagging and tests whether the evaluator has internalized the scope clause rather than treating every interactive element as needing input instructions.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent — applies only to controls associated with data entry; explicit scope clause excluding links and non-data-entry interactive components.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists, and there is no inapplicable/pass fixture in the corpus at all (testCaseCount 0). The techniques only demonstrate data-entry controls; nothing operationalizes the scope boundary that links/disclosure widgets are out of scope. The seed file is entirely failing data-entry patterns. Recognizing that a control is NOT a data-entry control — and therefore needs no 3.3.2 instruction — is a semantic/contextual judgment about each control's role and purpose that a naive checker (or an over-eager model) can get wrong by demanding labels everywhere. This is a precision/over-flagging guard that requires reasoning about what each control does.

references.quote: This success criterion does not apply to links or other controls (such as an expand/collapse widget, or similar interactive components) that are not associated with data entry.

The use of "requires" in this criterion's normative wording does not mean that the criterion only applies to required form fields... The criterion applies to all form fields, whether they're required or optional.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages that are dense with non-data-entry interactive controls (nav links, pagination, expand/collapse disclosures, tab strips, menu toggles, dialog-open buttons) that correctly carry NO field-style instructions — these should be judged PASS/inapplicable for 3.3.2. Include on most pages exactly one genuine data-entry field so the evaluator must distinguish in-scope from out-of-scope: in some pages that field is properly instructed (overall pass), in others it lacks instruction (the only true 3.3.2 failure on the page). The discriminating judgment is correctly NOT penalizing the non-input controls. Vision verification should confirm which controls are data-entry vs. action/navigation.
suggestedScenarios: Documentation page with many expand/collapse FAQ disclosures and a sidebar of nav links, plus one search field that IS properly labeled — only the disclosures/links are non-data-entry and correctly need no instruction (overall pass).
Article page with pagination links, a 'share' menu toggle, and breadcrumb links, none of which are data-entry — no 3.3.2 instruction is owed to any of them (inapplicable/pass for those controls).
Dashboard with tab strip, a 'Open settings' dialog-trigger button, and a 'Refresh' action button (no inputs) — all out of scope; the page should not be flagged for missing field instructions.
Mixed page where a correct, well-instructed newsletter email field coexists with many disclosure widgets and links — evaluator must pass the page and not demand instructions for the widgets.

Trap page: a control styled like an input (contenteditable div used purely as a read-only display, or a button visually resembling a text box) that is NOT a data-entry field — the evaluator must not demand a 3.3.2 instruction for it.

Discriminator page: many non-data-entry links/toggles plus ONE genuine data-entry field that DOES lack any instruction — the only correct 3.3.2 failure is that single field, and the links must not be flagged.

pages.scenario: Fintech (Tellard) wallet signup. The password field's only instruction is its complexity rules ('12+ chars, 1 number, 1 symbol'), deferred to a display:none div meant to reveal on focus. The reveal handler removes the WRONG class name (classList.remove('hide') instead of 'hidden'), a silent no-op, so the rules stay display:none in every state. On focus the field shows only empty space — the only instruction never appears.
pages.mechanism: The focus handler calls classList.remove('hide') on #pw-rules, but the hiding class is 'hidden'; remove() of an absent class is a no-op, so '.hidden{display:none}' is never lifted. The rules node stays display:none, is pruned from the AX tree, and the aria-describedby='pw-rules' association resolves to a hidden node — the field's only instruction is never perceivable on focus (or any state). Verified headless: hint stays display:none / rect 0x0 / not in viewport after driving keyboard focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct programmatic <label> ('Create password') and the rules node exists in the static DOM with real text plus an aria-describedby reference, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report a label-and-description present and pass it. No static checker drives focus, executes the handler to observe that classList.remove('hide') is a no-op leaving display:none in place, or judges that the only instruction never becomes perceivable. A scanner that merely confirms a hidden describedby node or a :focus rule exists would wrongly treat the instruction as provided — distinguishing 'instruction node exists' from 'instruction actually renders on focus' requires driving focus and visually judging the focused state.

pages.scenario: Brightleaf Coffee Co. checkout payment step. The promo-code field accepts only format 'ABC-1234' (three letters, dash, four digits) — the field's only instruction. The hint is revealed by a CSS '.promo-wrap:hover .promo-hint' rule ONLY; there is no :focus / :focus-within rule. A mouse user who hovers sees the format; a keyboard user who tabs to the field gets nothing.
pages.mechanism: Reveal is gated purely on :hover of the wrapper. On keyboard focus the hint stays opacity:0; max-height:0; overflow:hidden (collapsed, imperceptible). Verified headless: after page.focus(#promo) the hint reports opacity 0 / height 18 collapsed; only after page.hover(#promo) does it reach opacity 1 / height 50. Keyboard and most screen-reader users (who reach the field by focus, not hover) never receive the format instruction.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('Promo code'), so the form-label check passes, and the hint text plus a :hover reveal rule exist in the static stylesheet, so a static scan sees an instruction node and a reveal rule. Automated checkers do not distinguish a :hover trigger from a :focus trigger, do not drive keyboard focus to observe nothing reveals, and cannot judge that keyboard users never receive the instruction. Telling :hover apart from :focus and confirming the instruction is absent for keyboard users requires interaction (tabbing) and human judgment.

pages.scenario: Aerolink flight-booking date step. The travel-date field requires day-first format 'DD/MM/YYYY' — its only instruction. The hint is a 'floating help bar' (position:fixed; bottom:0) revealed on focus, but a booking-summary footer is ALSO position:fixed; bottom:0 with a higher z-index and opaque background. Both pin to the viewport bottom, so on focus the revealed hint paints directly behind the opaque footer and is fully occluded in every viewport.
pages.mechanism: #travel:focus ~ .date-hint sets display:block and the hint is visibility:visible/opacity:1 on focus, but .date-hint (position:fixed; bottom:0; z-index:10) and .summary-bar (position:fixed; bottom:0; z-index:50, opaque) share the bottom band, so the footer paints over the hint. Verified headless: after driving keyboard focus, document.elementFromPoint at the hint's center returns .summary-bar (not the hint) at viewports 800x600, 1024x768, 1280x900 and 1440x1024 — occlusion is deterministic across heights.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('Travel date'), so the form-label check passes; the hint node exists, transitions display:none->display:block on focus, and is wired via aria-describedby, so a static scan sees an instruction that 'appears on focus.' Automated checkers do not compute the painted stacking order of two competing position:fixed bottom bars, do not drive focus to render the focused state, and do not visually judge that the revealed instruction is hidden behind another element. Detecting the occlusion requires rendering the focused state and looking.

pages.scenario: Thornwood Makers community-forum signup. The username rules ('3-20 chars; letters/numbers/hyphens/underscores; must start with a letter') are the field's only instruction. On focus the tooltip fades in correctly, but a setTimeout(...,1500) then fades it out and sets aria-hidden while the field still has focus — it auto-dismisses before a slow reader finishes and does not return unless the field is blurred and re-focused.
pages.mechanism: The focus handler adds class 'show' then, 1500ms later, runs tip.classList.remove('show'); tip.setAttribute('aria-hidden','true') — dismissing the instruction during the same focus session, with no re-show on later interaction. Verified headless: after focus the tooltip is opacity:1 with real text; after waiting past 1.5s (field still focused) it is opacity:0 and aria-hidden. The aria-describedby target becomes hidden, so a re-querying screen reader finds nothing and a slow/magnifier user loses it mid-read.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('Choose a username'), so the form-label check passes; the instruction node exists, is shown on focus, and is wired via aria-describedby, so a DOM snapshot may even capture it visible. No automated checker measures how long an instruction stays perceivable, drives focus and waits 1.5s to watch it disappear, or judges that a timed auto-dismiss with no recovery path leaves the instruction effectively unavailable. Timing the appearance/disappearance and judging the window is too short requires interacting over time and human judgment.

pages.scenario: Faktura cross-border invoicing billing setup. The Tax-ID field requires a jurisdiction-specific format — its only instruction — delivered by a focus-revealed callout populated from the i18n string 'hint.taxid.format'. That key is missing from the en catalog and the templating layer's missing-key fallback is a single non-breaking space, so on focus a styled bordered box flicks into view but its entire content is U+00A0, conveying nothing.
pages.mechanism: #taxid:focus ~ .taxid-hint sets display:block and the box renders with padding/border on focus, but its only text node is a non-breaking space (the missing-i18n-key fallback). Verified headless: after focus the hint is display:block, in viewport, 450x38, but meaningfulChars=0 (text is only U+00A0). Screen readers following aria-describedby reach a node whose only content is a non-breaking space (announced 'blank'/a space); sighted users see a box that implies an instruction but states none.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('VAT / Tax identification number'), so this is not a missing-accessible-name case and the form-label check passes. The hint is not an empty element a linter would flag: its content is a non-breaking space (U+00A0), a non-empty text node, so whitespace-only/zero-length emptiness heuristics do not fire — many tools and AT explicitly count   as content. No automated checker reads the focus-revealed callout, recognizes that a non-breaking space carries no instruction, or judges the field's only instruction is meaningless; that requires reading the rendered focused state and a human judgment that U+00A0 is not an instruction.

The format instruction is present in the DOM and even associated via aria-describedby, but it is rendered inside a native <details> disclosure that is closed by default, so on the rendered page only a '? What format is required?' toggle is visible — the rule itself is display:none until clicked.

SC 3.3.2 requires instructions be presented to ALL users, not only AT users — the cue is orphaned from sighted users by disclosure state.

Tools do not evaluate a disclosure's open/closed state as a failure and cannot judge that the hidden content is a mandatory format rule sighted users need before typing. Screenshot confirmed: rendered page shows only the toggle, no format text.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).

The format instruction is present in the DOM, complete, sits directly beneath the field, and is wired with aria-describedby, but it is styled font-size:9px in #cdd4da on white (~1.5:1) — far below readable size/contrast. pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction is a complete sentence present in the DOM and associated via aria-describedby, so 'instruction exists/associated' passes. A contrast scanner may emit only a generic low-contrast note (1.4.3 has size carve-outs and tools key on computed style, not meaning) and cannot infer that the unreadable text is the field's required-format instruction and that 3.3.2 is consequently failed. Verified computed font-size=9px, contrast 1.5:1; screenshot shows a near-invisible smudge while the adjacent Group hint is legible.

citation.quote: Providing labels and instructions (including examples of expected data formats) helps all users — but particularly those with cognitive, language, and learning disabilities — to enter information correctly.

That readable, high-contrast format rule is collected into a 'Notes' block placed AFTER the 'Save and continue' submit button, so in both visual and DOM reading order it follows the action rather than informing the field; a user who fills the fields and clicks submit never sees it.
pages.mechanism: The field's format instruction is positioned after the submit action (and below the field it governs) in both visual and reading order, so it cannot inform the control at the point of entry; the user is forced into back-tracking the SC warns against. Verified: notes block follows the button in DOM order, is visually below the button, and is below the TIN field; TIN has no own adjacent hint.

citation.quote: Providing labels and instructions (including identification of required fields) can prevent users from making incomplete or incorrect form submissions, which prevents users from having to navigate once more through a page/form in order to fix submission errors.

pages.scenario: Credit-union 'Link an external bank account' form (Meridian Credit Union) laid out as a two-column CSS grid. pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every field has a proper visible label and the instruction text is present, readable, and high-contrast, so 'field labelled?' and 'instruction exists?' pass. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse reason about DOM order and programmatic association, not the rendered 2-D position of an instruction relative to multiple candidate fields in a CSS grid; they cannot compute which field a hint visually belongs to. Verified: routing hint top y=245 sits ~10px below the nickname field bottom (y=235) — same row band, beside a different field.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to have content authors present instructions or labels that identify the controls in a form so that users know what input data is expected.
